title: Elements of Statistical Computation
section: Summarizing \theta: Point Estimates from Loss Functions
text:
Summarizing \theta: Point Estimates from Loss Functions
The Bayes estimate minimizes the posterior expected loss: \hat\theta = \arg\min_{\hat\theta}\; E\big[L(\theta,\hat\theta)\mid y_{1:n}\big]







Loss L(\theta,\hat\theta)
Bayes estimate \hat\theta




(\theta-\hat\theta)^2 (squared error)
posterior mean E(\theta\mid y_{1:n})


\lvert\theta-\hat\theta\rvert (absolute error)
posterior median


I(\theta\ne\hat\theta) (0–1 loss)
posterior mode (MAP)



Interval estimate: a (1-\alpha) credible interval (\theta_{\alpha/2},\theta_{1-\alpha/2}) contains \theta with posterior probability 1-\alpha, a direct probability statement about \theta (unlike a confidence interval).
All of these are integrals or optimizations over the posterior, which is why Bayesian inference is computational.

title: Elements of Statistical Computation
text:
Prediction
The posterior predictive distribution of a new observation: P(y_{n+1}\mid y_{1:n}) = \frac{\int P(y_{n+1},y_{1:n}\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}{\int P(y_{1:n}\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}
If y_1,\ldots,y_n,y_{n+1} are conditionally independent given \theta, this simplifies to P(y_{n+1}\mid y_{1:n}) = \int P(y_{n+1}\mid\theta)\,P(\theta\mid y_{1:n})\,d\theta
an average of the sampling density over the posterior. With posterior draws \theta_1,\ldots,\theta_J\sim P(\theta\mid y_{1:n}), P(y_{n+1}\mid y_{1:n}) \approx \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J P(y_{n+1}\mid\theta_j)
The predictive distribution is wider than any single P(y_{n+1}\mid\theta_j): it carries both sampling variability and posterior uncertainty about \theta.

Prior
y_1,\ldots,y_n\mid\theta \overset{iid}{\sim}\text{Bern}(\theta), with \theta\sim\text{Beta}(\alpha_1,\alpha_0), \alpha_1,\alpha_0>0 given: \pi(\theta) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0+\alpha_1)}{\Gamma(\alpha_0)\Gamma(\alpha_1)}\,\theta^{\alpha_1-1}(1-\theta)^{\alpha_0-1}, \qquad 0<\theta<1
E(\theta) = \frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_0+\alpha_1}, \qquad
V(\theta) = \frac{\alpha_0\alpha_1}{(\alpha_0+\alpha_1)^2(\alpha_0+\alpha_1+1)}

\alpha_1 acts like a prior count of successes, \alpha_0 of failures; \alpha_0+\alpha_1 is the prior “sample size”
\text{Beta}(1,1) = \text{Unif}(0,1); \text{Beta}(2,1) has density 2\theta, favouring large \theta
Small \alpha’s give U-shaped or flat priors (vague); large \alpha’s concentrate the prior

title: Elements of Statistical Computation
text:
About the slides
The slides are written in Quarto and rendered with reveal.js. Every figure is drawn in R at render time, and the R code that produces a result is shown on the slide when the computation itself is the point; for illustrative figures the code is hidden but available in the source. Each example is self-contained: a data set is simulated with a fixed seed, so all numbers reported on the slides can be reproduced exactly by re-rendering. Where a method has a known failure mode, the slides show it rather than describe it, with a working example and a diagnostic. Derivations are kept on the slides in full, split across slides where they are long, and every lecture ends with a summary that connects the method to the ones before and after it.

title: Elements of Statistical Computation
text:
Topics
The course is organized around four computational tasks that recur throughout statistics.

Calculation

Why statistics needs computation: point estimation, hypothesis testing, and Bayesian inference as computational problems
Computer arithmetic: floating-point representation, overflow, underflow, rounding error, and stable formulas for variances and log-likelihoods



Simulation

Random number generation and elementary Monte Carlo: sampling distributions, evaluating estimators and tests by simulation
Rejection sampling: envelope functions, the uniform-under-the-curve view, adaptive rejection sampling for log-concave targets
Importance sampling: importance weights, self-normalized estimators, effective sample size and its limitations, applications to free energy and Bayesian cross-validation



Optimization

Maximum likelihood and numerical optimization: gradients and Hessians, Newton-type and gradient-based methods, visualizing curvature
The EM algorithm: the \(Q\) function, the ascending property, EM as alternating optimization, mixture models, censored data, and extensions to clustering, hidden Markov models, and factor analysis



Integration

Bayesian inference: prior, likelihood, posterior, posterior summaries as Bayes estimates under loss, prediction, the Beta–Bernoulli example
Numerical quadrature: midpoint, trapezoidal, and Simpson’s rules, transformations for infinite ranges, computing marginal likelihoods on the log scale, and the limits of quadrature in higher dimensions
Laplace approximation: Gaussian approximation at the posterior mode, the marginal likelihood and BIC, approximating posterior expectations
Markov chain Monte Carlo: Markov chains, invariance, detailed balance, Gibbs sampling and data augmentation, Metropolis–Hastings and step-size tuning, Metropolis-within-Gibbs, and an introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
